# Sabbāsava Sutta (MN 2 (PTS MN i 6))

**ID:** MN 2 (PTS MN i 6)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Sabbāsava Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 6  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sabbāsava Sutta* ("All the Defilements", MN 2; PTS MN i 6) is the second discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*. In this discourse, the Buddha explains that the destruction of the defilements (*āsavas*, or "outflows") is realized through knowing and seeing (*jānato ahaṁ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṁ khayaṁ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato*) rather than by ignorance [Galasek 2016]. Rather than prescribing a single remedy for every spiritual difficulty, the Buddha explains that different defilements require different approaches, outlining seven distinct methods for abandoning them: by seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, and developing. For instance, certain defilements are abandoned through the proper use of robes and other requisites, which are utilized upon wise reflection simply to protect against cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things [Nattier 2003]. Modern scholars note that the sutta demonstrates the Buddha's internalization and reinterpretation of ethical concepts, reacting against and providing a counterargument to earlier Jain ascetic notions of physical *āsavas* [Galasek 2016].

 In later canonical literature, the sutta is cited in the *Sāriputtasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 16) and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 2.2, Kv 2.3).
